Critical slowing down (τ→∞)

Words: 49
Bifurcation theory OurBigBook.com
Critical slowing down is the divergence of a relaxation time as a stable equilibrium point approaches loss of hyperbolicity. For a scalar ordinary differential equation it occurs when f′(N∗)↑0 and the recovery time of a stable equilibrium −1/f′(N∗) diverges. At the threshold, nonlinear terms may replace exponential decay by algebraic decay; for example N′=−kN3 has N(t)∼(2kt)−1/2 for positive initial data.

Bifurcation parameter

Words: 52
Bifurcation theory OurBigBook.com
A bifurcation parameter labels a family of dynamical systems in which a qualitative change of equilibria or other invariant sets is studied. Near a simple critical eigenvalue crossing, a nonzero derivative with respect to the physical control parameter permits using that eigenvalue itself as a local parameter. At a codimension-two bifurcation, two independent parameters are generally needed.

Global bifurcation

Words: 70
Bifurcation theory OurBigBook.com
A global bifurcation changes an invariant set through a global orbit connection or collision that cannot be identified by a single equilibrium point's linearization alone. For example, a global bifurcation through a saddle homoclinic orbit occurs when an outgoing unstable separatrix returns to the same saddle equilibrium's stable manifold. A smooth global Poincaré return map then combines with a local passage map to determine which side contains a periodic orbit. A heteroclinic orbit instead joins distinct equilibrium points; an energy-balance or Melnikov integral can locate its breaking in a nearly Hamiltonian system.

Neimark–Sacker bifurcation (λ1,2​=e±iθ,d=0)

Words: 211 Articles: 2
Bifurcation theory OurBigBook.com
A Neimark–Sacker bifurcation of a smooth planar map occurs when a simple complex-conjugate pair of fixed-point Floquet multipliers crosses the unit circle away from low-order resonances. If its radial normal form is r′=r(1+η+dr2)+⋯ with d=0, a small invariant closed curve has r2=−η/d+⋯. For d<0 it appears on η>0, where the fixed point has become unstable, and its radial Floquet multiplier is 1−2η+⋯, so the bifurcation is supercritical. For d>0 the curve lies on η<0 and is unstable, giving a subcritical bifurcation. Area-preserving maps have a vanishing cubic radial drift at an elliptic point and do not meet this dissipative nondegeneracy condition.

Cubic radial coefficient of a quadratic planar map (ℓ=Re(λg21​))

Words: 59
Neimark–Sacker bifurcation OurBigBook.com
In a complex coordinate write z′=λz+f20​z2+f11​zz+f02​z2, with ∣λ∣=1. Away from strong resonances of a planar map, the quadratic change z=w+h20​w2+h11​ww+h02​w2 has h20​=f20​/(λ2−λ), h11​=f11​/(1−λ) and h02​=f02​/(λ2−λ). Substituting and collecting w2w gives g21​=2f20​h11​+f11​h20​+f11​h11​+2f02​h02​. The cubic radial coefficient is ℓ=Re(λg21​); ℓ<0 gives a supercritical crossing when the multiplier modulus increases through one.

Strong resonance of a planar map (λk=1,k≤4)

Words: 59
Neimark–Sacker bifurcation OurBigBook.com
At a strong resonance of a planar map the Floquet multiplier of a fixed point is a root of unity of low order. The usual nonresonant Neimark–Sacker bifurcation requires λk=1 for k=1,2,3,4. At a 1:3 resonance a quadratic term z2 cannot be removed from the normal form; at a 1:4 resonance a cubic term z3 remains. Consequently one cannot infer a quasiperiodic invariant curve from the unit-modulus crossing alone.

Bifurcation

Words: 26
Bifurcation theory OurBigBook.com
A bifurcation is a qualitative change in the phase portrait of a dynamical system as a parameter varies, for example creation of equilibrium points or a change in their stability.

Normal form (dynamical systems)

Words: 194 Articles: 2
Bifurcation theory OurBigBook.com
A simplified local vector field obtained by smooth changes of state variables, and sometimes time or parameter, retaining the terms that cannot be removed at the required order. Near a simple zero eigenvalue, reduction to a centre manifold can give the transcritical form v˙=ϵv−v2 or a reflection-symmetric pitchfork form x˙=ϵx±x3. The nonzero leading coefficients and permitted coordinate changes are part of the classification.

Quadratic even-odd mode interaction

Words: 62
Normal form (dynamical systems) OurBigBook.com
A reflection acting as (A,B)↦(A,−B) forces an equivariant vector field to have A˙ even and B˙ odd in B. With the zero solution preserved, its quadratic normal form is A˙=λ1​A+a1​A2+a2​B2, B˙=λ2​B+a3​AB. For positive coefficients, every mixed equilibrium with B=0 has Jacobian determinant −2a2​a3​B2<0, hence is a saddle equilibrium. The two invariant-axis equilibria meet in a transcritical bifurcation, and the mixed branches meet them in pitchfork bifurcations.

Near-identity transformation (x=y+h(y),Dh(0)=0)

Words: 65
Normal form (dynamical systems) OurBigBook.com
A near-identity transformation is a local change of variables whose derivative at the reference point is the identity. In a normal form of a dynamical system, substituting x=y+h(y) and solving (I+Dh(y))y˙​=f(y+h(y)) determines which nonlinear coefficients can be removed. The transformation is locally invertible by the inverse function theorem. Terms whose removal equations are singular are resonant and must be retained; a computed zero resonant coefficient cannot be assigned an arbitrary nonzero value by normalization.

Steady-state bifurcation (detDx​f(x0​,μ0​)=0)

Words: 64
Bifurcation theory OurBigBook.com
A change in local branches or stability of equilibrium points of a dynamical system as a parameter varies. A zero Jacobian eigenvalue is necessary for the equilibrium-branch bifurcations of a smooth finite-dimensional system: without it, the implicit function theorem gives a unique nearby equilibrium branch. It is not sufficient by itself; nonzero coefficients in the reduced normal form of a dynamical system establish the bifurcation type. A Hopf crossing has nonzero imaginary eigenvalues and is a different local bifurcation.

Subcritical bifurcation

Words: 57
Bifurcation theory OurBigBook.com
A subcritical branch emerges on the parameter side where the original state remains stable. In the cubic Landau amplitude equation A˙=μA−g∣A∣2A with g<0, the small nonzero branch lies at μ<0 and is unstable to radial amplitude perturbations. Higher-order saturation can generate a finite-amplitude stable branch and hysteresis, but this does not follow from a cubic truncation alone.

Supercritical bifurcation

Words: 64
Bifurcation theory OurBigBook.com
A supercritical branch emerges on the parameter side where the original state loses stability. In the cubic Landau amplitude equation A˙=μA−g∣A∣2A with g>0, the nonzero branch ∣A∣2=μ/g lies at μ>0 and is stable to radial amplitude perturbations. Continuous phase symmetry still leaves a neutral phase direction. The direction of a branch and its stability should both be checked in a general problem of bifurcation theory.

Codimension-two bifurcation

Words: 1k Articles: 13
Bifurcation theory OurBigBook.com
A codimension-two bifurcation requires two independent parameter conditions to hold simultaneously. Simultaneous stationary and Hopf bifurcation thresholds require both kinds of critical mode in the reduced amplitude equation. A crossing of modes at different wavenumbers is different from a zero-frequency double-zero degeneration of one fixed-wave-number cubic.

Cusp bifurcation (x˙=β1​+β2​x−x3)

Words: 70
Codimension-two bifurcation OurBigBook.com
A cusp is a two-parameter degeneracy at which two saddle-node bifurcation curves meet and the reduced steady equation has a triple root. In the displayed scalar normal form, simultaneous vanishing of the polynomial and its derivative gives β2​=3x2, β1​=−2x3. Thus the folds satisfy 4β23​=27β12​, with β2​≥0. Between the folds there are three real equilibria, and outside them one. A transverse stable direction may be present in a higher-dimensional realization.

Fold-Hopf bifurcation (λ0​=0,λ±​=±iω,ω=0)

Words: 130 Articles: 1
Codimension-two bifurcation OurBigBook.com
A fold-Hopf bifurcation combines a simple zero eigenvalue and a nonzero imaginary pair at an equilibrium point. In a three-dimensional centre manifold, a normal form of a dynamical system separates a real fold amplitude from a complex oscillatory amplitude. A rotationally symmetric normal form permits reduction to two real amplitude equations, while the oscillation phase continues to evolve. Secondary bifurcations of the amplitude flow can produce invariant tori in the full dynamical system.

First integral of the quadratic fold-Hopf amplitude flow (F=−u(λ2​+u2/3+v2))

Words: 70
Fold-Hopf bifurcation OurBigBook.com
The amplitude equations u′=−2uv, v′=λ2​+v2+u2 satisfy u′=Fv​, v′=−Fu​, hence preserve the displayed first integral. For λ2​=−a2<0 and u≥0, the centre equilibrium is (a,0) with F=2a3/3, while the two boundary saddle equilibria are (0,±a) with F=0. The level F=0 contains the boundary connection and the arc u2=3(a2−v2) joining the two saddle equilibria. Levels 0<F<2a3/3 form closed periodic orbits. Adding an independent rotating phase turns these closed amplitude trajectories into invariant tori.

Saddle-node separatrix-loop bifurcation

Words: 96
Codimension-two bifurcation OurBigBook.com
A saddle-node separatrix-loop point occurs when a saddle-node equilibrium simultaneously has a global returning separatrix at its strong stable manifold. In the local form x˙=x2−μ, y˙​=−λy, a global return to y=h at x=ν makes the codimension-two point μ=ν=0. For μ>0 a saddle loop occurs on ν=μ​. The saddle-node boundary μ=0 has an invariant-circle segment on the ν<0 side, while for ν>0 a nearby periodic orbit avoids the bottleneck and survives the local equilibrium fold. The return geometry, rather than the local saddle-node normal form alone, determines the global orbit.

Bogdanov–Takens bifurcation

Words: 605 Articles: 7
Codimension-two bifurcation OurBigBook.com
A Bogdanov–Takens bifurcation has a double zero eigenvalue with a nontrivial Jordan block and generic two-parameter unfolding. Its local diagram includes saddle-node bifurcations, Hopf bifurcations, and a curve of small homoclinic orbits. A weakly perturbed Hamiltonian scaling can locate the homoclinic curve through energy balance.

Quadratic-product flow with a double-zero bifurcation (u˙=u(μ+u−v),v˙=λ(u2−v))

Words: 185 Articles: 1
Bogdanov–Takens bifurcation OurBigBook.com
For λ>0, the equilibrium points are the origin and (s,s2) with s=(1±1+4μ​)/2. The nonzero branches have Jacobian trace s−λ and determinant λs(2s−1). They have a saddle-node bifurcation at μ=−1/4, s=1/2; the origin exchanges stability with the lower branch at the transcritical bifurcation μ=0. A Hopf bifurcation occurs on the upper branch at μ=λ(λ−1) for λ>1/2. The point (μ,λ)=(−1/4,1/2) has a double zero eigenvalue and a nontrivial Jordan block. Its generic unfolding includes a saddle-loop curve and the intervening stable periodic orbit region.
Quadratic escape desingularization
Words: 106
Quadratic-product flow with a double-zero bifurcation OurBigBook.com
For u˙=u(μ+u−v), v˙=λu2 in u>0, the time change dτ/dt=u gives the affine linear system uτ​=μ+u−v, vτ​=λu. Shifting w=v−μ removes the forcing. Its eigenvalues are (1±1−4λ​)/2. For λ>1/4, putting ω=4λ−1​/2 gives
u(τ)=eτ/2[hcos(ωτ)+ωμ+h/2−v0​​sin(ωτ)].
(1)
For fixed μ>0 and initial h,v0​ tending to zero, the first return to small positive u occurs after approximately π/ω=2π/4λ−1​. This is a half-turn, not a full turn. At λ=1/4, u=eτ/2[h+(μ+h/2−v0​)τ] does not return and grows without bound. The loss of return diagnoses escape to infinity rather than a finite-amplitude homoclinic orbit. Physical time obeys dt=dτ/u and need not share the divergent desingularized travel time.

Quadratic Bogdanov–Takens unfolding (x˙=y,y˙​=−λ+μy+x2+xy)

Words: 69
Bogdanov–Takens bifurcation OurBigBook.com
For λ>0, the equilibrium points are x=±λ​, y=0. The positive branch is a saddle; the negative branch has a subcritical Hopf bifurcation at μ=λ​. A homoclinic orbit occurs at μ=(5/7)λ​+O(λ) near the double-zero point. Between this homoclinic curve and the Hopf curve, an unstable periodic orbit surrounds a stable equilibrium point. The factor 5/7 follows from a Melnikov energy-balance method, using the integrals of v2 and uv2 along the leading conservative saddle loop.

Reflection-symmetric cubic double-zero normal form (q˙​=p,p˙​=−λq+κp+σq3−2σq2p)

Words: 309 Articles: 3
Bogdanov–Takens bifurcation OurBigBook.com
The sign σ=±1 distinguishes an inverted quartic potential from a double-well potential. The origin has determinant λ and trace κ. Nonzero equilibria obey q2=λ/σ, with determinant −2λ and trace κ−2λ. Its energy p2/2+λq2/2−σq4/4 has derivative (κ−2σq2)p2. The origin's Hopf bifurcation is supercritical for σ=1 and subcritical for σ=−1. In the latter case the nonzero equilibria have supercritical Hopf bifurcations at κ=2λ<0.

Nilpotent cubic damping invariant (b=g21​+3f30​)
Words: 159 Articles: 1
Reflection-symmetric cubic double-zero normal form OurBigBook.com
For a reflection-symmetric vector field u˙=v+f30​u3+f21​u2v+⋯, v˙=g30​u3+g21​u2v+⋯, introduce x=u, y=u˙. Differentiating gives x˙=y and a cubic acceleration with x2y coefficient b=g21​+3f30​. The contribution 3f30​ comes from differentiating the first equation's cubic term. Further cubic near-identity transformations can remove nonresonant terms but cannot turn b=0 into a nonzero coefficient by a nonsingular scaling. This is a useful check before assigning a generic reflection-symmetric Bogdanov–Takens bifurcation to a calculated Taylor expansion.

Hamiltonian blow-up of a reflection-symmetric double-zero point (H=u2+sv2/2−v4/8)
Words: 77
Reflection-symmetric cubic double-zero normal form OurBigBook.com
Near a nilpotent origin with σ=1, μ=0, the weighted scaling uold​=ε2u, vold​=εv, τ=εt, μold​=ε2μ, σ=1+ε2s makes the leading cubic confinement flow u′=−sv+v3/2, v′=2u. Steady–Hopf mode interaction

Words: 135
Codimension-two bifurcation OurBigBook.com
For a chosen orientation and phase-reduced steady amplitude a and nonresonant oscillatory amplitude z, a schematic normal form is a˙=rs​a−gs​a3−hs​a∣z∣2, z˙=(ro​+iω0​)z−go​∣z∣2z−ho​a2z. For rs​,gs​>0 the pure steady branch exists and is radially attracting; its oscillatory perturbation is damped when ro​−ho,r​rs​/gs​<0, where ho,r​=Re(ho​). For ro​,go,r​>0, go,r​=Re(go​), the pure oscillatory branch exists and is radially attracting; its steady perturbation is damped when rs​−hs​ro​/go,r​<0. The transverse inequalities are not existence or full stability tests by themselves. Mixed intensities u=a2>0, v=∣z∣2>0 solve gs​u+hs​v=rs​, ho,r​u+go,r​v=ro​. Their intensity Jacobian matrix has trace −2(gs​u+go,r​v) and determinant 4uv(gs​go,r​−hs​ho,r​), giving attraction in intensities when the trace is negative and determinant positive. Resonant phases, oppositely travelling modes or zero-frequency limits need additional retained amplitudes; this schematic pair is not a universal complete normal form.

Stationary bifurcation

Words: 23
Bifurcation theory OurBigBook.com
At a stationary bifurcation, a real eigenvalue of the linearized system passes through zero. Nearby equilibria may then be created, destroyed, or exchange stability.

Amplitude equation

Words: 2k Articles: 30
Bifurcation theory OurBigBook.com
An amplitude equation describes the slow evolution of the coefficient of a critical mode near an instability threshold. Symmetry and solvability determine its leading nonlinear terms.

Conserved-mean convection amplitude equations (Aτ​=νA−3∣A∣2A−2∣B∣2A)

Words: 70
Amplitude equation OurBigBook.com
The partial differential equation Tt​=−μΔT−Δ2T+∇⋅(∣∇T∣2∇T) on a 2π-periodic square conserves the spatial mean. On a fixed-mean subspace its first instability is at μ=1 and has four real critical amplitudes. With μ=1+ε2ν and T=ε(Aeix+Beiy+complex conjugate)+⋯, projection onto the critical Fourier modes gives the displayed equation and its A,B interchange. For ν>0, squares have ∣A∣2=∣B∣2=ν/5, amplitude eigenvalues −2ν,−2ν/5, and neutral translation phases. Rolls have a positive transverse growth rate ν/3.

Conserved-field real amplitude equation (AT​=μA+αA2−A3+AXX​−AB,BT​=σ(B+δA2)XX​)

Words: 210 Articles: 2
Amplitude equation OurBigBook.com
With periodic boundary conditions, the spatial mean of B is a conserved quantity. For zero mean write B=HX​ with periodic zero-mean H. The functional V=⟨μA2/2+αA3/3−A4/4−AX2​/2−A2HX​/2−HX2​/(4δ)⟩ generates AT​=δV/δA, HT​=2δσδV/δH. Thus VT​=⟨AT2​+HT2​/(2δσ)⟩≥0. Completing the square in HX​ bounds V above by a coercive quartic polynomial when 0<δ<1, ruling out nonconstant recurrent motion on regular precompact trajectories.

Coexistence fraction of a conserved-field amplitude mesa (h=4δα29(1−δ)2μ​+2δ1−δ​)

Words: 74
Conserved-field real amplitude equation OurBigBook.com
For 0<δ<1 and α=0, a broad localized plateau in the conserved-field real amplitude equation has effective parameter ν=μ−δ⟨A2⟩ and stationary equation A′′+νA+αA2−(1−δ)A3=0. Equal endpoint values of its first integral give R=2α/[3(1−δ)], ν=−2α2/[9(1−δ)]. If the plateau occupies fraction h of a long periodic interval, ⟨A2⟩≃hR2 supplies the displayed relation. It applies when both the plateau and exterior are long relative to the front width; 0<h<1 gives its leading existence interval.

Periodic stability criterion for a conserved-field uniform amplitude (r>0,(π/L)2+r−2δR2>0,r=R(2R−α))

Words: 73
Conserved-field real amplitude equation OurBigBook.com
A nonzero uniform equilibrium of the conserved-field real amplitude equation obeys μ=R2−αR. Fixed zero mean excludes the constant B perturbation. Its homogeneous amplitude eigenvalue is −r. For a nonzero Fourier wavenumber k, the stability matrix has trace −r−(1+σ)k2 and determinant σk2(k2+r−2δR2). The displayed conditions are necessary and sufficient for strict linear stability on a period 2L. In an infinite-domain limit the nonzero-mode condition becomes r≥2δR2; a long-wave instability need not occur in a sufficiently short domain.

Directly forced cubic amplitude equation (AT​=(μ+iΛ)A−∣A∣2A+1)

Words: 124 Articles: 1
Amplitude equation OurBigBook.com
A forcing at the carrier wavenumber breaks continuous spatial translation symmetry and adds a constant to its complex amplitude equation. In a frame following a moving forcing pattern, its phase drift gives iΛA. A nonzero forcing coefficient is normalized to one by scaling amplitude by its cube root and time by its two-thirds power. A steady intensity s=∣A∣2 satisfies s[(μ−s)2+Λ2]=1, and its phase is uniquely determined by the steady complex equation.

Fold and Hopf thresholds of a directly forced cubic amplitude (Λcusp​=3​/2,ΛH,min​=2−1/3)

Words: 54
Directly forced cubic amplitude equation OurBigBook.com
For the directly forced cubic amplitude equation, a saddle-node bifurcation requires Λ2=1/s−1/(4s4) and μ=s+1/(2s2). The right side has its unique maximum 3/4 at s=1, giving a cusp bifurcation at (Λ,μ,s)=(3​/2,3/2,1). The stability matrix has trace 2(μ−2s) and determinant (μ−3s)(μ−s)+Λ2. A Hopf bifurcation requires μ=2s, s(s2+Λ2)=1 and Λ2−s2>0. These imply Λ>2−1/3; equality is a double-zero linear degeneracy rather than an ordinary Hopf bifurcation.

Parametrically forced counterpropagating waves (AT​=μA+νB−βA∣A∣2−γA∣B∣2)

Words: 112 Articles: 1
Amplitude equation OurBigBook.com
Two counterpropagating modes transform as (A,B)↦(eikδA,e−ikδB) under spatial translation. Forcing at twice their natural frequency breaks continuous temporal phase symmetry but preserves simultaneous sign reversal. Hopf bifurcation

Words: 2k Articles: 12
Bifurcation theory OurBigBook.com
A Hopf bifurcation creates or destroys a small periodic orbit near an equilibrium point as a pair of complex conjugate eigenvalues crosses the imaginary axis. It explains how a resting state can give way to sustained oscillations: the linearization of a dynamical system supplies rotation and growth, while a nonlinear term can saturate that growth at a nonzero amplitude.
The simplest supercritical Hopf bifurcation is the exact Hopf normal form
z˙=(μ+iω)z−∣z∣2z,z=x+iy,ω>0.
(6)
Here z is a complex number, μ is the bifurcation parameter, and ω is the angular frequency. In polar coordinates z=reiθ, the equations become r˙=μr−r3 and θ˙=ω for r>0. At μ<0, each turn shrinks towards the equilibrium point. At μ>0, small radii grow and large radii shrink towards r=μ​, producing a limit cycle. For example, μ=0.04 and ω=2 give radius 0.2, period π, and frequency 1/π cycles per unit time. The limiting angular frequency stays nonzero while the amplitude tends to zero: a tiny newborn oscillation can still repeat at a finite rate.
For a precise generic statement, consider a smooth function f defining an autonomous differential equation x˙=f(x,α) on Rn, with a smooth branch of equilibrium points x∗​(α) and critical parameter α=0. Require:
  • the Jacobian matrix Dx​f(x∗​(α),α) to have a simple pair of eigenvalues β(α)±iω(α), with β(0)=0 and ω(0)>0;
  • every other eigenvalue to have nonzero real part at α=0;
  • a transverse crossing, β′(0)=0;
  • a nonzero cubic radial coefficient a=Reℓ(0)=0 in the reduced Hopf normal form.
Then a locally unique branch of small periodic orbits, up to phase, emerges on the side βa<0. On the two-dimensional centre manifold, the branch attracts for a<0 and repels for a>0. Attraction in the full phase space additionally requires all remaining eigenvalues to have negative real part; any transverse unstable direction makes the periodic orbit unstable there.[ref]
An eigenvalue-crossing bifurcation test alone cannot establish these nonlinear conclusions. For example, the purely linear equation z˙=(μ+iω)z has the same crossing but no isolated periodic orbit: at μ=0 every nonzero radius is constant, and at μ=0 none is. If the cubic coefficient vanishes, higher-order terms must be examined; a generalized Hopf bifurcation is one possible degeneracy. The usefulness of the generic theorem is that a large system can have its small oscillatory onset understood through one Hopf normal form, subject to these hypotheses and local limits.

Hopf bifurcation OurBigBook.com
A generalized Hopf bifurcation has a vanishing cubic radial coefficient and nonzero quintic coefficient. The two parameters unfold the eigenvalue real part and cubic coefficient. With R=r2, periodic orbits satisfy τ+aR+bR2=0. Their saddle-node bifurcation curve is τ=a2/(4b) with R=−a/(2b)>0, hence ab<0. For b>0 the smaller-radius limit cycle is stable and the larger one unstable where both exist; their collision explains why the criticality change of a Hopf bifurcation curve brings a saddle-node bifurcation of periodic orbits.

Supercritical Hopf bifurcation (r˙=μr−r3)

Words: 183
Hopf bifurcation OurBigBook.com
In a supercritical Hopf bifurcation, a small periodic orbit attracts within the critical centre manifold on the side where the equilibrium point repels within that manifold. Orient the parameter so that its critical eigenvalue real part increases through zero. For the exact Hopf normal form z˙=(μ+iω)z−∣z∣2z, with ω>0, the nonzero constant radius solves
0=μr−r3,r∗​=μ​(μ>0).
(7)
For 0<r<r∗​ the radius grows; for r>r∗​ it shrinks. A radial disturbance δr therefore has leading equation δr˙=−2μδr, since ∂r​(μr−r3)∣r∗​​=−2μ<0. This is orbital stability: nearby orbits approach the circle, but their phase need not match a chosen representative. The exact angular frequency is ω, so the period is 2π/ω and the frequency is ω/(2π).
The Jacobian matrix at zero is (μω​−ωμ​), with eigenvalues μ±iω. Zero attracts for μ<0 and repels for μ>0. Exactly at μ=0, r˙=−r3 gives
r(t)=1+2r02​t​r0​​,t≥0.
(8)
Thus zero still has asymptotic stability in this model, with algebraic decay, and there is no nonzero limit cycle at the threshold itself. As μ↓0 on the cycle branch, both its radius μ​ and its radial attraction rate 2μ vanish. Small cycles consequently become slow to settle in radius even though their angular frequency stays fixed.

Hopf normal form (z˙=(μ+iω)z+ℓz∣z∣2+⋯)

Words: 299
Hopf bifurcation OurBigBook.com
The Hopf normal form is a local normal form of a dynamical system on the critical two-dimensional centre manifold. After shifting the equilibrium point and changing coordinates, its cubic truncation can be written
z˙=(μ+iω(μ))z+(a+ib)z∣z∣2,r˙=μr+ar3,θ˙=ω(μ)+br2,
(9)
where μ is the critical eigenvalue real part, a=Reℓ(0), b=Imℓ(0), and ω(0)>0. Smooth parameter dependence of the cubic coefficients and higher-order terms are omitted in this truncation. The real coefficient a controls radial saturation; the imaginary coefficient b changes the angular frequency with amplitude. This finite-order reduction, rather than literal equality to a cubic equation everywhere, is the meaning of the Hopf normal form for a general system.[ref]
In the cubic truncation, r∗2​=−μ/a whenever μa<0. Substituting into the angular equation gives Ω=ω(μ)−bμ/a. For the full smooth system, the leading normal form radius satisfies r∗2​=−μ/a+o(∣μ∣) and the period tends to 2π/ω(0). The exact circle and exactly constant angular frequency of the special model a=−1, b=0, ω(μ)=ω are conveniences of that model. In the original coordinates the small periodic orbit need not be a circle. Radial scaling can normalize a nonzero a to −1 or +1, so ∣μ∣​ is a normalized leading amplitude, not a universal physical radius.

Subcritical Hopf bifurcation

Words: 209
Hopf bifurcation OurBigBook.com
In a subcritical Hopf bifurcation, the small periodic orbit repels within the critical centre manifold and lies on the side where the equilibrium point attracts within that manifold. With the critical eigenvalue real part increasing through zero, the positive cubic sign gives the exact radial Hopf normal form
r˙=μr+r3,θ˙=ω>0.
(10)
For μ<0, the nonzero radius is r∗​=−μ​. Radii below r∗​ shrink to zero, whereas radii above it grow. The radial derivative at the cycle is μ+3r∗2​=−2μ>0, proving that the periodic orbit repels. For example, μ=−0.04 gives an unstable circle of radius 0.2: a radius of 0.1 decays while one of 0.3 grows. The unstable circle shrinks into zero as μ↑0; at μ=0, r˙=r3 already drives every small positive radius outward.
For μ>0 there is no nonzero constant radius in this cubic model, and zero repels. In a general dynamical system, this says only that the nearby orbits leave the local neighbourhood. It does not guarantee a distant attracting limit cycle, a jump to a particular amplitude, or hysteresis. Additional nonlinear or global information is needed; the quintic radial Hopf equation illustrates one possible stabilizing extension. Reversing the parameter orientation reverses which numerical side contains the branch, so the defining distinction between supercritical Hopf bifurcation and subcritical Hopf bifurcation is their reduced stability and their relation to the equilibrium point, rather than the bare sign of an arbitrarily named parameter.
